[[MI1|MI1(b)]] was a department of [[British Military Intelligence]] set up during [[World War I]] for the interception and [[cryptanalysis]] of coded messages. Unlike its equivalent in the Admiralty, [[Room 40]], where women were employed in clerical roles, MI1(b) employed women as linguists, translators, and cryptanalysts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bruce |first=James |date=2017-04-16 |title='A shadowy entity': M.I.1(b) and British Communications Intelligence, 1914–1922 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02684527.2016.1270992 |journal=Intelligence and National Security |language=en |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=319 |doi=10.1080/02684527.2016.1270992 |issn=0268-4527|url-access=subscription }}</ref> By 1919, a third of MI1(b)’s civilian cryptanalysts and linguists were women.<ref name=":0">Bruce (2017), p. 326.</ref>

Most of MI1(b)'s female codebreakers are known to have been university-educated, and several came from teaching backgrounds. Some of them had previously served in the [[Hush WAACs]], a small group of codebreakers working near the front lines in France in 1917–18, and some went on to work at the [[Government Code and Cypher School]], formed in 1919 to continue codebreaking work during peacetime. At least one member, [[Emily Anderson]], also worked as a codebreaker during [[World War II]] at [[Bletchley Park]].

At first, recruitment to MI1(b) was done on a basis of personal contact, with women being selected for their knowledge of languages, particularly German. In 1917, the fourteen-strong staff of MI1(b) under the leadership of [[Malcolm Vivian Hay]] moved to new premises at Cork Street and its workforce expanded.<ref name=":1">Bruce (2017), p. 319.</ref> Recruitment became more formal and Hay introduced his own testing for candidates who applied.<ref name=":0" /> Details are limited due to the destruction of records, both accidental and deliberate, pertaining to MI1(b).<ref>Bruce (2017) p. 313.</ref>

== Women known to have worked at MI1(b) ==
Women known to have worked at MI1(b) are (in alphabetical order):

=== Emily Anderson ===
{{Main|Emily Anderson}}
Emily Anderson (1891–1962) was an Irish translator and music historian who was Professor of German at [[University of Galway|University College Galway]] when she was called on by the war effort for her language skills. Initially trained for the Hush WAACs, she instead took a post at MI1(b) in July 1918. In 1920, she joined GC&CS at the rank of Junior Assistant along with Florence Hayllar. Head of the Italian Diplomatic Section, she became a trainer of other decoders. Her decoding work continued throughout the 1930s and 1940s, including [[Women in Bletchley Park|service at Bletchley Park]]. She was awarded an [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] in 1943.

=== Miss J.F. Carleton and Miss Chichester ===
Miss J.F. Carleton and Miss Chichester are known to have been working for MI1(b) as linguists or cryptanalysts at the time of its change of premises in 1917.<ref name=":1" /> Miss Chichester worked on Uruguayan, Spanish, and Argentine codes.<ref name=":2">Norburn, Bryony, ''The Role of Female Cryptanalysts from 1914 to 1946'' (PhD thesis, 2021), p. 401.</ref> J.F. Carleton worked on American codes, and went on to become a Junior Assistant at GC&CS.<ref>Norburn (2021), p. 361; 401.</ref>

=== Florence Mabel Hannam ===
Florence Mabel Hannam was [[Mentioned in dispatches|mentioned in despatches]] for her service as a Hush WAAC, for which she won the Victory Medal and the British War Medal in 1919.<ref name=":3">Norburn (2021), p. 204.</ref><ref name="roll">{{cite web |title=Hush WAAC Roll of Honour |url=https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/hush-waac-roll-honou |access-date=15 May 2024 |website=www.gchq.gov.uk |language=en}}</ref> She worked at MI1(b) on non-alphabetical Romanian field codes,<ref name=":2" /> and then at GC&CS from 1918 to 1920.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chionna |first=Jackie Ui |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dFRsEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22claribel+spurling%22&pg=PT61 |title=Queen of Codes: The Secret Life of Emily Anderson, Britain's Greatest Female Code Breaker |date=2023-04-13 |publisher=Headline |isbn=978-1-4722-9548-4 |pages=47 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Florence Hayllar ===
Florence Hayllar Hayllar<ref>Hayllar's middle name and surname were identical.</ref> (b. 1868) was a professional writer from Brighton.<ref name=":4">Norburn (2021), p. 209.</ref> A university graduate, she published poetry collections<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hayllar |first=Florence |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WKGeDAEACAAJ |title=The Legend of Saint Frideswide and Other Poems |date=2016-05-17 |publisher=Creative Media Partners, LLC |isbn=978-1-356-78662-6 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hayllar |first=Florence H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iaYDAAAAQAAJ&q=florence+hayllar |title=Camilla and Gertrude: And Other Poems |date=1884 |publisher=White |language=en}}</ref> and a novel<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hayllar |first=Florence |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KO4jvgAACAAJ |title=Nepenthes |date=2016-05-21 |publisher=Creative Media Partners, LLC |isbn=978-1-358-40263-0 |language=en}}</ref> as well as articles on social issues.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ellis |first=Havelock |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WH9_EAAAQBAJ&dq=florence+hayllar+aggravating&pg=PT116 |title=The Task of Social Hygiene |date=2022-08-01 |publisher=DigiCat |language=en}}</ref> She was editor of the linguistics journal [[Notes and Queries]] from 1912 to 1942.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LDrKo33V0wMC&q=florence+hayllar |title=The Periodical |date=1941 |publisher=Oxford University Press |pages=228 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Page:Notes and Queries - Series 11 - General Index.djvu/7 - Wikisource, the free online library |url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Notes_and_Queries_-_Series_11_-_General_Index.djvu/7 |access-date=2024-07-30 |website=en.wikisource.org |language=en}}</ref>

Hayllar served as a Hush WAAC and joined MI1(b) in 1917.<ref name=":5">Chionna (2023), pp. 53–4.</ref><ref name="Norburn 2021, p. 94">Norburn (2021), p. 94.</ref> While at MI1(b), she composed poetry mocking the sexist attitudes of her male colleagues<ref name=":5" /> and expressing a hope that the 'shadowy Entity' of MI1(b) would be lent form by memory one day.<ref name=":1" />

She was appointed Junior Assistant at GC&CS in January 1920 along with Emily Anderson, and left the position after a month.<ref>Chionna (2023), p. 68.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ferris |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XxUvEAAAQBAJ&dq=florence+hayllar&pg=PA62 |title=Behind the Enigma: The Authorised History of GCHQ, Britain's Secret Cyber-Intelligence Agency |date=2021 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing PLC |isbn=978-1-5266-0548-1 |pages=62 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" />

=== Barbara Freire-Marreco ===
{{Main|Barbara Freire-Marreco}}
The 'Miss Marreco' known to have worked on Spanish, French, German and South American codes for MI1(b) was probably Barbara Freire-Marreco (1879–1967), an anthropologist known for her fieldwork among the [[Puebloans|Pueblo]] peoples. She also worked for the War Trade Intelligence Department during WWI.<ref name="Norburn 2021, p. 94"/>

=== Alda Milner-Barry ===
{{Main|Alda Milner-Barry}}
[[Alda Milner-Barry]] (1893–1938) worked as a translator in the Intelligence Department of the War Office in 1916 after studying Medieval and Modern Languages at [[Newnham College, Cambridge]]. After a stint as a German professor, she started work at MI1(b) in 1917. She was deputy to Emily Anderson. After the war she worked as an English lecturer and vice-principal of Newnham College.<ref>Chionna (2023), pp. 43–4.</ref>

=== Claribel Spurling ===
{{Main|Claribel Spurling}}
[[Claribel Spurling]] (1875–1941) was a headmistress and German teacher at [[Birkenhead High School Academy|Birkenhead High School]] when her brother was killed in action in 1917, and she subsequently joined the [[Women's Royal Naval Service|WRNS]]. She is known for being the only person to score 100% on a supposedly impossible test set for candidates for the expanded MI1(b) by Major Hay. She worked on German, French, and Italian codes, and went on to work at GC&CS as a Junior Assistant. After her codebreaking career she worked as a warden of several university halls and co-wrote children's stories and drama with [[Beatrice Clay]].<ref>Norburn (2021), pp. 207–221.</ref>

=== Gwendoline Watkins ===
Gwendoline Edith Gwyllyam Watkins (b. 1895) was one of the first six women to be selected as a Hush WAAC for her 'somewhat rusty' knowledge of German, and the youngest of the group at the age of twenty-two.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Watkins |first=G. E. |url=https://collection.nam.ac.uk/detail.php?q=searchType%3Dsimple%26resultsDisplay%3Dlist%26acc%3D1998-01-110&pos=0&total=1&page=1&acc=1998-01-110-1 |title=Memories of a Hushwaac in France |pages=1}}</ref><ref name="roll" /> She was [[Mentioned in dispatches|mentioned in despatches]] for her work in France, and was awarded the Victory Medal and the British War Medal in 1919.<ref name=":3" /> After nine months working at the War Office at the close of the war,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Typescript memoirs of G E G Watkins, Women's Army Auxiliary Corps {{!}} Online Collection {{!}} National Army Museum, London |url=https://collection.nam.ac.uk/detail.php?q=searchType=simple&resultsDisplay=list&acc=1998-01-110&pos=0&total=1&page=1&acc=1998-01-110-1 |access-date=2024-07-30 |website=collection.nam.ac.uk}}</ref> she, like her fellow WAAC Florence Hannam, worked at MI1(b) on Romanian non-alphabetical field codes and at GC&CS, departing in 1920.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chionna |first=Jackie Ui |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dFRsEAAAQBAJ&dq=florence+hannam+cryptanalyst&pg=PT61 |title=Queen of Codes: The Secret Life of Emily Anderson, Britain's Greatest Female Code Breaker |date=2023-04-13 |publisher=Headline |isbn=978-1-4722-9548-4 |language=en}}</ref>
